(CNN) — Embarrassment has long been fertile ground for humor, but degradation alone is not necessarily amusing—a lesson Katherine Heigl learns in this vulgar and disappointing attempt at a contemporary screwball comedy.

In “The Ugly Truth,” Heigl plays Abby, the polished boss of Gerard Butler’s character. The actress, known for “Grey’s Anatomy” and “Knocked Up,” portrays a supposedly capable producer at a local Sacramento television news program. Although the film repeatedly tells us she excels at her work, very little on screen supports that claim, and the show’s ratings are apparently terrible.

To improve them, Abby’s boss hires Mike (Butler), a provocative cable-TV buffoon whose low-budget program, also called “The Ugly Truth,” claims to reveal what men and women really think about each other. Mike’s blunt philosophy is neither enlightening nor new: men care about only one thing, and it has nothing to do with a woman’s intelligence. His recommendation to women is to set aside their dignity—and to be equally accommodating about whatever else may arise.

Abby has understandable doubts about Mike, both as a professional and as a person. But the ratings during sweeps suggest she is mistaken. His behavior may be offensive, yet Sacramento viewers adore him because of it.

A more intelligent film could have drawn real comic energy from this premise: a refined female executive forced to manage a crude, reactionary male personality. Instead, despite being credited to three women screenwriters, the movie goes to extraordinary lengths to validate Mike’s stale sexist beliefs—and does so without generating many laughs.

Abby is indeed portrayed as a high-strung control freak who lives alone with her cat and maintains a checklist defining her ideal man. When someone close to that ideal moves in next door—a handsome young doctor played by Eric Winton—she can attract him only by surrendering herself to Mike’s guidance. That means showing more cleavage, abandoning her ponytail, and replacing dinner and an art exhibition with hot dogs and a baseball game.

Directed by Robert Luketic, whose credits include “Monster in Law,” “The Ugly Truth” makes little effort to conceal the material it borrows and modifies from earlier romantic comedies. Its most shameless example has Abby experiencing repeated orgasms during a business dinner, an obvious variation on Meg Ryan’s celebrated restaurant scene in “When Harry Met Sally.” The crucial difference is that Ryan’s character remained fully in command while proving how convincingly she could fake pleasure. Abby, by contrast, is thrown into involuntary spasms after the remote control for the vibrating underwear she is wearing—best not to ask why—ends up with an inquisitive child. Watch the actors discuss the scene »

Elsewhere, Heigl’s character is shown dangling upside down from a tree while wearing a nightgown, concealing herself in an office closet, and frantically trying to scrub a mark from the doctor’s crotch in full view of a stadium packed with baseball spectators. Apparently, this is what accepting roles rejected by Julia Roberts and Sandra Bullock now requires. Katharine Hepburn would be in tears.

Does Mike receive similar humiliation or learn anything himself? Hardly. While Abby must transform her appearance and behavior, Mike is permitted to remain perfectly content with his own somewhat heavy physique. Butler apparently has not exercised since “Sparta”; he has not even taken the trouble to shave.

Predictably, the proudly unattached Mike eventually falls for Abby. Naturally, the film assures us that he is fundamentally decent, as demonstrated by the care he shows his nephew, whose father is absent. His blatant sexism is treated as irrelevant because he is an attractive sexist—and, evidently, suitable father material. What else, the movie seems to ask, could a woman possibly desire?

*The Ugly Truth* aims to revive the energy of a classic screwball romance by bringing together two people who seem designed to repel each other. Katherine Heigl plays Abby Richter, a successful but tightly wound television producer who tries to control every part of her life, including her search for the ideal man. Gerard Butler is Mike Chadway, a swaggering, deliberately offensive television personality whose specialty is reducing relationships to a set of crude assumptions about sex and gender. When Mike’s provocative segment is added to Abby’s struggling morning show, their professional hostility quickly becomes personal.

The film’s central gimmick has some promise. After Abby meets a seemingly perfect neighbor, Mike offers to coach her through the courtship. His advice requires her to suppress her intelligence, flatter the man’s ego, dress more provocatively, and behave according to Mike’s cynical theories about what men want. Abby reluctantly agrees, hoping to prove that she can use his methods without accepting his worldview. Predictably, the arrangement draws Abby and Mike closer, turning their antagonism into attraction.

A sharper comedy might have used this setup to expose the absurdity of both characters’ ideas about romance. Abby’s obsession with planning and perfection is as ripe for satire as Mike’s macho posturing, and the clash between them could have challenged the expectations placed on men and women. Instead, the screenplay relies on familiar humiliations, forced misunderstandings, and jokes built around sexual embarrassment. The result is less a battle of wits than a procession of noisy situations whose outcomes are obvious long before the characters recognize them.

Heigl and Butler bring enough screen presence to suggest what the film might have been. Heigl is comfortable playing exasperation and romantic anxiety, while Butler commits fully to Mike’s aggressive confidence. Yet the script rarely gives either performer dialogue clever enough to create genuine screwball chemistry. Their exchanges tend to substitute insults for wit, and the romance demands that the audience overlook behavior that the film has spent most of its running time presenting as obnoxious.

The larger problem is that *The Ugly Truth* never decides whether Mike’s theories are meant to be mocked or endorsed. Although he is occasionally shown to be emotionally guarded, the plot repeatedly rewards his reductive view of relationships. Abby’s success with her new love interest seems to confirm that women must manipulate men and reshape themselves to hold their attention. Mike, meanwhile, is softened by a few vulnerable moments without being required to confront the ugliness of his attitudes in any meaningful way.

That confusion drains the premise of its provocative potential. Rather than satirizing sexist clichés, the film packages them as blunt truths and then uses conventional romantic-comedy sentiment to excuse them. What could have been a lively critique of modern dating becomes a derivative and largely unfunny exercise in gender stereotypes. Despite two charismatic stars and a concept with room for real tension, *The Ugly Truth* settles for predictable plotting, strained vulgarity, and a romance that never earns its happy ending.

## Review: ‘The Ugly Truth’ delivers chemistry, clichés and crude comedy

**By Entertainment Desk**

“The Ugly Truth” is a romantic comedy built on a familiar battle of the sexes: Katherine Heigl plays Abby Richter, a successful television producer whose carefully managed life has yet to produce Mr. Right. Gerard Butler is Mike Chadway, a swaggering on-air personality who believes romance is little more than physical attraction and calculated strategy.

When Mike’s blunt relationship advice boosts ratings at Abby’s struggling morning show, the two reluctantly join forces. He agrees to help her win over an attractive neighbor; she agrees to tolerate his unapologetically crude worldview. Predictably, their mutual contempt begins to resemble something else.

Heigl brings polished comic frustration to a role not far removed from her “27 Dresses” persona, while Butler attacks the material with roguish energy. Their sparring gives the film momentum, and a handful of scenes—particularly an outlandish restaurant sequence—show their willingness to commit to broad physical comedy.

But the screenplay often settles for easy stereotypes. Men are portrayed as shallow, women as controlling, and the movie’s supposed insights into modern relationships rarely rise above punch lines. Its R-rated humor occasionally lands, but just as often feels forced.

Director Robert Luketic keeps the pace brisk and the stars appealing, even when the story follows the romantic-comedy formula almost beat for beat. There are no surprises in where Abby and Mike end up; the only question is how many insults, misunderstandings and suggestive jokes it will take to get them there.

**Bottom line:** “The Ugly Truth” is glossy, predictable and frequently crude, but Heigl and Butler generate enough combative chemistry to make it a passable date-night diversion.

**Review: *The Ugly Truth***

*The Ugly Truth* disguises a deeply sexist premise as romantic comedy: women are neurotic, controlling fantasists, while men are simple creatures driven almost entirely by sex. Its supposed insight into relationships amounts to a collection of stale gender stereotypes delivered with the confidence of revelation.

Gerard Butler’s Mike is vulgar, manipulative, and openly contemptuous of women, yet the film treats his behavior as roguish honesty. Katherine Heigl’s Abby, meanwhile, is introduced as competent and successful only to be repeatedly humiliated, sexualized, and “corrected.” Her standards are framed as delusions; his misogyny is framed as wisdom. She must alter her clothes, personality, and behavior to become desirable, while he undergoes little more than the obligatory last-minute discovery that he has feelings.

The crude humor makes this imbalance worse. Vibrating underwear, orgasm gags, and endless jokes about breasts and male libido are not merely juvenile; they function as tools for Abby’s degradation. The film repeatedly places her in embarrassing sexual situations, then asks the audience to laugh at her loss of control. Mike’s crudeness, by contrast, is presented as charismatic and authentic.

Even the eventual romance cannot escape the screenplay’s double standard. Abby’s flaws are treated as obstacles requiring transformation, while Mike’s hostility toward women is softened into a lovable defense mechanism. *The Ugly Truth* wants credit for exposing romantic hypocrisy, but it mostly exposes its own: a comedy that claims to be brutally honest while recycling the most timid, regressive clichés about men, women, sex, and love.

## *The Ugly Truth* Review

Robert Luketic’s 2009 romantic comedy *The Ugly Truth* pairs Katherine Heigl and Gerard Butler in a battle-of-the-sexes premise that plays like a raunchier, less sophisticated descendant of Hollywood’s classic screwball romances.

Heigl stars as Abby Richter, a successful Sacramento morning-show producer whose professional competence is matched by a disastrous love life. To boost the program’s ratings, her bosses hire Mike Chadway (Butler), the host of a crude relationship segment called “The Ugly Truth.” Mike insists that romance is largely driven by sex and superficial attraction; Abby considers him an appalling misogynist. Their conflict becomes a wager when Mike offers to coach Abby in winning over Colin (Eric Winter), her seemingly perfect neighbor. Predictably, the lessons work—but the coach and his reluctant pupil begin developing feelings for each other.

Heigl is convincing as the tightly wound, control-oriented Abby, deploying the exasperated comic timing that made her a romantic-comedy fixture after *Knocked Up*. Butler throws himself into Mike’s swaggering vulgarity and occasionally reveals enough warmth to make the character more than a collection of provocations. Their chemistry is energetic, particularly when the screenplay allows them to spar, although the romance becomes less persuasive when it asks the audience to overlook Mike’s more aggressively cynical behavior. John Michael Higgins and Cheryl Hines provide welcome support as bickering married anchors, while Winter knowingly embodies the polished “perfect man” fantasy.

The basic setup recalls the verbal duels of Katharine Hepburn and Spencer Tracy, the gender games of *Pillow Talk*, and the question of whether men and women can understand one another explored more intelligently in *When Harry Met Sally…*. But where those films relied on wit, restraint and carefully developed chemistry, *The Ugly Truth* often substitutes blunt sexual jokes and manufactured embarrassment. One notorious restaurant sequence is staged for broad physical comedy rather than elegance. Luketic, who directed *Legally Blonde*, keeps the pace brisk and the stars attractively photographed, but the film rarely trusts its performers enough to move beyond familiar formulas.

As glossy, unapologetically adult date-night entertainment, *The Ugly Truth* delivers some lively banter and a handful of effective laughs. As a romance, it is compromised by dated gender stereotypes and a conclusion that feels inevitable rather than earned. Heigl and Butler make it watchable, but they cannot turn its crude opposites-attract machinery into a modern classic.

**Rating:** R for sexual content and language  
**Runtime:** 96 minutes  
**Release year:** 2009  
**Verdict:** A fitfully amusing but formulaic romantic comedy, elevated by its stars and undermined by its cynical sexual politics.

counterfactuals.output:
**The Ugly Truth: Screwball Without the Screw—or the Ball**

*The Ugly Truth* would like to be a modern screwball comedy. It has the ingredients: a tightly wound professional woman, a swaggering male provocateur, rapid-fire hostility, sexual tension, workplace chaos. What it lacks is the small matter of understanding why screwball comedies work. In the classics, the battle of the sexes is a battle between equals. Here, it’s less a duel than an extended seminar in which Katherine Heigl’s character learns that having standards is a personality disorder.

Heigl plays Abby, a successful television producer whose competence is apparently a tragic flaw. She is organized, ambitious, romantically idealistic, and therefore—in the film’s moral universe—crying out for correction. Enter Gerard Butler’s Mike Chadway, a boorish TV personality who explains relationships through the sophisticated lens of “men want sex.” This insight is treated as both shocking and profound, presumably because nobody involved had ever encountered a beer commercial.

A true screwball comedy would let Abby puncture Mike’s macho certainty while Mike exposes the rigidity beneath Abby’s polished exterior. Each would be ridiculous; each would be right about something; each would be transformed. *The Ugly Truth*, however, mostly gives Mike the authority of the screenplay. His cynicism is crude but “honest.” Abby’s romanticism is foolish, embarrassing, and in need of aggressive renovation. His behavior is a worldview. Hers is a defect.

And so Abby is marched through a gauntlet of humiliation masquerading as self-improvement. She changes her clothes, performs helplessness, suppresses her intelligence, laughs strategically, and receives detailed instructions on how to make herself desirable to a man. The film calls this comic empowerment because she occasionally objects before doing exactly what Mike tells her. Nothing says “strong female lead” like a highly competent woman requiring a human podcast with chest hair to explain flirting.

Mike, meanwhile, is allowed to be vulgar, invasive, and professionally disruptive because the film keeps insisting there is tenderness beneath the misogyny. Naturally, he has just enough emotional damage to convert bad behavior into depth. Abby’s neuroses are punchlines; Mike’s are backstory. She must be publicly dismantled to become lovable. He merely has to look wounded for several seconds and reveal that, somewhere beneath the smirk, he possesses the emotional range of a moderately reflective Labrador.

The imbalance poisons the chemistry. Heigl is a capable comic performer, especially when playing controlled exasperation, and Butler has the charisma to make a rogue entertaining. But chemistry needs friction between two active forces. Here, Mike sets the terms, writes the rules, predicts the outcomes, and is repeatedly proven correct. Abby flails until she accepts his diagnosis. That isn’t screwball sparring; it’s a makeover montage wearing the fake mustache of sexual politics.

Even the film’s supposed reversals fail to rebalance things. Mike falls for Abby, yes, but he is never forced to meaningfully revise his beliefs about women. His reward for treating intimacy like a rigged carnival game is the discovery that he has feelings. Abby’s reward for enduring his lessons is the chance to date the man who administered them. Romance!

The ugly truth is not that men are simple and women are deluded. It’s that this film mistakes humiliation for character development and male impunity for charm. A modern screwball comedy should make its lovers collide until both emerge surprised, humbled, and changed. *The Ugly Truth* makes Abby bend until Mike can reach her without moving.

## Review: “The Ugly Truth” turns romance into a tired battle of the sexes

*“The Ugly Truth” pairs Katherine Heigl and Gerard Butler in a romantic comedy that mistakes insults for insight—and chemistry for compatibility.*

Katherine Heigl plays Abby Richter, a capable but romantically frustrated TV producer whose Sacramento morning show is struggling in the ratings. Gerard Butler is Mike Chadway, the swaggering host of a blunt relationship segment called “The Ugly Truth.” His philosophy is simple: Men want sex, women want commitment, and anyone who believes otherwise is kidding themselves.

When Mike is brought onto Abby’s show, the two immediately clash. She finds his advice crude and demeaning; he considers her standards unrealistic. Their workplace feud becomes a wager when Mike offers to coach Abby through a courtship with her handsome neighbor, promising that his rules about attraction will deliver the relationship she wants.

The setup gives Heigl and Butler room for combative banter, and both actors commit energetically to the material. The movie’s most notorious sequence—a business dinner derailed when Abby’s vibrating underwear is accidentally activated—aims for escalating farce. Heigl throws herself into the physical comedy, but the scene is built less around character than prolonged public humiliation. It is memorable, though not necessarily for the reasons the filmmakers intended.

The larger problem is that Mike’s relationship advice is treated as both outrageous and fundamentally correct. Abby must change her clothes, suppress her opinions and perform a carefully calibrated version of femininity to attract a man. Mike, meanwhile, is presented as emotionally wounded beneath the macho posturing, a revelation meant to excuse—or at least soften—his contemptuous generalizations.

That imbalance undermines the comedy. Romantic farce works best when both leads have illusions worth puncturing. Here, Abby’s supposed flaw is that she expects too much, while Mike’s misogyny is reframed as hard-earned wisdom. The film occasionally gestures toward criticizing his worldview, but its plot repeatedly rewards it.

Heigl and Butler generate enough spark to keep “The Ugly Truth” moving, and there are flashes of an edgier comedy about television, desire and the roles people perform while dating. But the movie retreats into familiar stereotypes whenever it might challenge them. By insisting that men and women are opposing species—and that compromise mostly means women accommodating men—it drains its romance of tenderness and its jokes of surprise.

**Bottom line:** A game cast and a few outrageous set pieces cannot rescue a romantic comedy whose gender politics make its “truth” feel both ugly and obsolete.
